content: 1. In 1982, three maternity hospitals in Pelotas, a city in southern Brazil, were visited daily to identify live births. A total of 5,914 liveborn infants whose families resided in the urban area of the city were examined, and their mothers were interviewed. Data on maternal and child health, family socioeconomic conditions, and pregnancy complications were collected during the perinatal study. These participants have been followed up multiple times, and in 2012-2013, cohort members were invited to visit the study clinic. 2. The Nurses' Health Study, initiated in 1976, included 121,700 female nurses aged 30-55 years residing in 11 large U.S. states. Participants were enrolled via questionnaires and followed biennially until 1986 to assess risk factors for breast cancer, the occurrence of breast cancer, and other major illnesses. A final analysis included 89,413 parous women. Exclusion criteria included a prior history of cancer (except nonmelanoma skin cancer), lack of lactation history, nulliparity or missing parity information, and women with children under 4 years of age at enrollment or later births unless specific conditions (e.g., age ≥45, tubal ligation, or menopause) were met to avoid bias related to reduced breastfeeding after a breast cancer diagnosis. 3. The Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study recruited pregnant women across Norway at 18 weeks of gestation. From 6 to 18 months of age, mothers reported breastfeeding status at four intervals (6-8, 9-11, 12-14, and 15-18 months). Median values for each interval were used to calculate breastfeeding duration. Breastfeeding was defined as any breastfeeding, regardless of the introduction of solids or formula. The primary outcome was the presence of current asthma at 7 years, determined by prescription data indicating at least two prescriptions within a 12-month period. 4. The Women's Health Initiative, a large prospective study addressing morbidity and mortality among postmenopausal women, excluded participants with a history of cancer (except nonmelanoma skin cancer), no follow-up information, prevalent self-reported diabetes at baseline, or missing data on parity and breastfeeding. The final analytic sample included 136,652 women. Data on parity and breastfeeding characteristics were collected at baseline via self-administered questionnaires, including the number of pregnancies, term pregnancies, age at first term pregnancy, breastfeeding history, number of children breastfed, and total months of breastfeeding. The primary outcome was the incidence of diabetes during follow-up, determined by self-reported new diagnoses treated with insulin or oral hypoglycemic medications. 5. The 45 and Up Study in Australia randomly selected participants from the Medicare database. Women aged 45 years or older who had given birth between 18 and 45 years of age and had not undergone a hysterectomy or bilateral oophorectomy were included. Breastfeeding duration was calculated by dividing the total breastfeeding duration by the number of children for each woman. Women were classified as having high blood pressure if they reported being treated for it in the past month. 6. The TARGet Kids. study in Toronto, Canada, recruited healthy urban children aged 1 to 6 years attending routine primary healthcare visits between December 2008 and June 2011. Data were collected prospectively through standardized parent-completed surveys. Children who had never been breastfed were classified as having a total breastfeeding duration of 0 months, while those currently breastfeeding were classified based on the child’s current age. The primary outcome was iron deficiency, defined as serum ferritin levels <14 mcg/L. 7. The Carnegie Survey, conducted between 1937 and 1939 in Britain, collected cross-sectional data on diet, social circumstances, and health from 2,995 subjects (60%) from 1,072 families. Data on infant feeding methods and breastfeeding duration were obtained from mothers for each child aged 0-19 years. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into intervals (e.g., two weeks to <two months, >two to <six months, >six to <12 months, >12 months, and unknown). Outcomes included mean differences in z-scores for height, trunk length, and leg length. 8. The Ryukyus Child Health Study (RYUCHS) in Okinawa, Japan, included 38,212 schoolchildren aged 6-15 years from public elementary and junior high schools in Naha and Nago Cities. Data were collected via questionnaires completed by parents or students. The analysis included 24,077 students, focusing on the prevalence of allergic disorders in the past 12 months. Outcomes included wheezing, atopic eczema, and rhinoconjunctivitis. Exclusion criteria included missing or illogical data on the factors under investigation. 9. The Nurses’ Health Study cohort (1976) followed 89,887 women biennially from 1986 until a diagnosis of breast cancer, death, or June 1, 1992. Exclusion criteria included death before 1986, a history of cancer (except nonmelanoma skin cancer) between 1978 and 1986, nulliparity or unknown parity status, lack of breastfeeding history, and in-situ breast cancer. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as never, <1 month to 48 months, and unknown. 10. The Muniz 2015 study analyzed all live births from 1982 and 1993 in Pelotas, Brazil. Data on breastfeeding duration and infant feeding methods were collected. Outcomes included anthropometric measures and health indicators.
